frequentist confidence interval. For a symmetric unimodal posterior the equal-tailed and HPD intervals
coincide; for skewed posteriors the HPD interval is shorter but can be harder to compute from samples,
so equal-tailed intervals (posterior sample quantiles) are the common default. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Markov chain Monte Carlo {#sec-mcmc}

Outside the conjugate families the posterior @eq-bayes is known only up to the intractable normalizing
constant $p(\mathbf y)$, and posterior expectations $\mathbb{E}[g(\boldsymbol\xi) \mid \mathbf y]$ are
high-dimensional integrals with no closed form. Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sidesteps both problems
by constructing a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is the posterior; running the chain
produces dependent draws whose ergodic averages estimate posterior expectations. The construction needs
only the *ratio* of posterior densities, in which $p(\mathbf y)$ cancels. We develop the general theory
on an abstract state space and then specialize to the posterior.

::: {#def-markov-kernel}
## Transition kernel and stationary distribution
A *transition kernel* on a measurable state space $(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{B})$ is a map $P: \mathcal{X}
\times \mathcal{B} \to [0,1]$ such that $P(x, \cdot)$ is a probability measure for each $x$ and
$P(\cdot, B)$ is measurable for each $B$. A probability measure $\pi$ on $\mathcal{X}$ is *stationary*
(or invariant) for $P$ if
$$
\int_{\mathcal{X}} P(x, B)\, \pi(dx) = \pi(B) \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.
$$
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

Stationarity is the property that, if the chain's current state is distributed as $\pi$, then so is its
next state; a chain started anywhere and run long enough (under further ergodicity conditions) forgets
its start and produces draws from $\pi$. The practical way to guarantee a prescribed stationary
distribution is the stronger and easier-to-check condition of detailed balance.

::: {#def-detailed-balance}
## Detailed balance (reversibility)
A transition kernel $P$ is *reversible* with respect to a probability measure $\pi$, or satisfies
*detailed balance*, if the two measures on $\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{X}$ defined by $\pi(dx)P(x, dy)$
and $\pi(dy)P(y, dx)$ are equal:
$$
\pi(dx)\, P(x, dy) = \pi(dy)\, P(y, dx).
$$ {#eq-detailed-balance}
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation.** Detailed balance says the long-run flow of probability from $x$ to $y$ exactly
matches the flow from $y$ back to $x$, for every pair of states. Nothing circulates on net, so once the
chain is distributed as $\pi$ it stays that way: $\pi$ is held in place. It is a stronger condition than
stationarity but far easier to check (a pointwise equation instead of an integral one), which is why
every sampler in this chapter is engineered to satisfy it. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#lem-detailed-balance-stationary}
## Detailed balance implies stationarity
If $P$ satisfies detailed balance with respect to $\pi$ (@def-detailed-balance), then $\pi$ is
stationary for $P$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Fix $B \in \mathcal{B}$. Integrate the detailed-balance identity @eq-detailed-balance over $x \in
\mathcal{X}$ and $y \in B$. The left side is
$$
\int_{\mathcal{X}} \int_{B} \pi(dx)\, P(x, dy) = \int_{\mathcal{X}} P(x, B)\, \pi(dx),
$$
which is the quantity in @def-markov-kernel. The right side is
$$
\int_{\mathcal{X}} \int_{B} \pi(dy)\, P(y, dx) = \int_{B}\left(\int_{\mathcal{X}} P(y, dx)\right)\pi(dy)
= \int_{B} P(y, \mathcal{X})\, \pi(dy) = \int_{B} 1 \cdot \pi(dy) = \pi(B),
$$
using $P(y, \mathcal{X}) = 1$ because $P(y, \cdot)$ is a probability measure, and Tonelli's theorem to
exchange the order of integration of the nonnegative kernel. Equating the two sides gives
$\int_{\mathcal{X}} P(x, B)\, \pi(dx) = \pi(B)$ for every $B$, which is stationarity. $\square$
:::

The Metropolis-Hastings algorithm builds a reversible kernel for any target $\pi$ from an arbitrary
proposal mechanism, correcting the proposal by an accept-reject step.

::: {#thm-mh-stationarity}
## Metropolis-Hastings has the target as stationary distribution
Let $\pi$ be a target density on $\mathcal{X}$ with respect to a reference measure, and let $q(x, y)$ be
a proposal density (so $q(x, \cdot)$ is a density for each $x$). Define the acceptance probability
$$
\alpha(x, y) = \min\!\left\{1, \; \frac{\pi(y)\, q(y, x)}{\pi(x)\, q(x, y)}\right\}
$$ {#eq-mh-acceptance}
for $x, y$ with $\pi(x)q(x, y) > 0$, and the Metropolis-Hastings kernel
$$
P(x, dy) = \alpha(x, y)\, q(x, y)\, dy + r(x)\, \delta_x(dy), \qquad
r(x) = 1 - \int \alpha(x, y)\, q(x, y)\, dy,
$$
where $\delta_x$ is the point mass at $x$ (the probability of rejecting and staying). Then $P$ satisfies
detailed balance with respect to $\pi$, and hence (by @lem-detailed-balance-stationary) $\pi$ is
stationary for $P$.
:::

::: {.proof}
The kernel has two parts: a "move" part with density $p(x, y) = \alpha(x, y)\, q(x, y)$ for $y \ne x$,
and a "stay" part, the atom $r(x)\delta_x$. We check the detailed-balance identity @eq-detailed-balance
for each.

*Move part.* We must show $\pi(x)\, p(x, y) = \pi(y)\, p(y, x)$ for all $x \ne y$, that is
$$
\pi(x)\, q(x, y)\, \alpha(x, y) = \pi(y)\, q(y, x)\, \alpha(y, x).
$$
Fix $x \ne y$. If either $\pi(x)q(x,y) = 0$ or $\pi(y)q(y,x) = 0$ the identity holds trivially (both
sides are $0$, since $\alpha$ multiplies the vanishing factor). Otherwise both products are positive,
and the ratio $\rho = \pi(y)q(y, x)/(\pi(x)q(x, y))$ is a positive real with $\alpha(x, y) = \min\{1,
\rho\}$ and $\alpha(y, x) = \min\{1, 1/\rho\}$. Suppose $\rho \le 1$ (the case $\rho > 1$ is symmetric by
swapping $x$ and $y$). Then $\alpha(x, y) = \rho$ and $\alpha(y, x) = 1$, so
$$
\pi(x)\, q(x, y)\, \alpha(x, y) = \pi(x)\, q(x, y)\, \rho = \pi(x)\, q(x, y)\cdot \frac{\pi(y)\, q(y, x)}{\pi(x)\, q(x, y)}
= \pi(y)\, q(y, x) = \pi(y)\, q(y, x)\, \alpha(y, x),
$$
as required. Thus $\pi(x)p(x, y)\, dx\, dy$ is symmetric in $(x, y)$.

*Stay part.* The atomic contribution to $\pi(dx)P(x, dy)$ is $\pi(x)\, r(x)\, \delta_x(dy)\, dx$, a
measure concentrated on the diagonal $\{x = y\}$. The diagonal is invariant under the coordinate swap
$(x, y) \mapsto (y, x)$, and on it $\pi(x)r(x)\delta_x(dy)\,dx = \pi(y)r(y)\delta_y(dx)\,dy$ because both
describe the same mass $\pi(x)r(x)$ placed at $x = y$. Hence the stay part also satisfies detailed
balance.

Adding the move and stay parts, $\pi(dx)P(x, dy) = \pi(dy)P(y, dx)$, so $P$ is reversible with respect
to $\pi$. By @lem-detailed-balance-stationary, $\pi$ is stationary. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
Two practical points. First, the acceptance ratio @eq-mh-acceptance involves $\pi$ only through the
ratio $\pi(y)/\pi(x)$, in which the normalizing constant $p(\mathbf y)$ cancels; this is what makes MCMC
applicable to the unnormalized posterior. Second, stationarity alone does not guarantee that the time
average $\frac1N \sum_{t=1}^N g(\boldsymbol\xi^{(t)})$ converges to $\mathbb{E}_\pi[g]$; that requires
the chain to be $\pi$-irreducible (it can reach any set of positive $\pi$-measure) and aperiodic, under
which a law of large numbers for Markov chains gives almost-sure convergence of ergodic averages and a
central limit theorem (under further conditions such as geometric ergodicity) governs the Monte Carlo
error. We state this ergodic theorem as a cited result (@tierney1994) and use it to justify Monte Carlo
estimation; its proof belongs to the general theory of Harris-recurrent chains. The original
symmetric-proposal algorithm is due to @metropolis1953 and the general asymmetric form to @hastings1970. (Corresponds to the
Metropolis-Hastings content of L.3 in the proof catalogue.) $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**What this means in practice, and what to check.** The theory above guarantees only that the chain
*eventually* produces draws from the posterior; it says nothing about any particular finite run. It helps
to picture what the software hands back. When you fit a Bayesian meta-analysis or NMA, the sampler returns
a long list of draws $\boldsymbol\xi^{(1)}, \boldsymbol\xi^{(2)}, \dots$, and each draw is one complete,
jointly plausible setting of every parameter at once: each pooled effect $d_{1k}$, the heterogeneity
$\tau^2$, and every study-level contrast. A posterior mean is then just the average of one column of that
list, a $95\%$ credible interval is a pair of sample quantiles, and a treatment ranking is computed draw
by draw and tallied. Plotted against iteration, a single parameter's *trace* should look like a fuzzy
horizontal band (a "grassy" caterpillar), not a slow drift or a path that sticks in one place for long
stretches. Before trusting any of these numbers, check four things: (i) *convergence*, that several
chains started from different points overlap, summarized by the potential scale reduction factor $\hat R$
lying near $1$; (ii) the *effective sample size*, the number of effectively independent draws after
discounting autocorrelation, which must be large enough that the *Monte Carlo error* (the sampler's own
noise, distinct from genuine posterior uncertainty) is negligible; (iii) *divergent transitions*,
warnings that the sampler could not follow the posterior geometry and that estimates may be biased; and
(iv) *prior sensitivity*, that the conclusions do not swing with an arbitrary choice of prior. Theoretical
correctness (detailed balance) and a trustworthy run (clean diagnostics) are separate matters, and an ITC
result needs both. These diagnostics are developed in full in the Bayesian-computation chapter of Part V.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and the No-U-Turn Sampler {#sec-hmc}

Random-walk Metropolis explores by undirected local steps and mixes slowly in high dimensions, because
the proposal must be small to be accepted yet small steps decorrelate slowly. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
(HMC) replaces the random walk by deterministic trajectories that follow the gradient of the log
posterior, allowing distant, high-acceptance proposals. It is the sampler inside Stan and the engine of
the ML-NMR software of Part V.

The physical picture is worth carrying through the algebra that follows. Imagine the negative log
posterior $-\log\pi(\boldsymbol\xi \mid \mathbf y)$ as a landscape, with deep valleys where the posterior
is high. HMC gives the current parameter value a random shove (a *momentum*) and lets it roll across this
landscape under Newtonian mechanics for a short while, then proposes wherever the roll ends. Because the
motion follows the gradient, it travels *along* a valley rather than diffusing across it, so one proposal
can land far from the start yet still in a plausible region, which is exactly what random-walk Metropolis
cannot do in high dimensions. The *kinetic energy* $K(\mathbf r)$ is the cost of moving, the *potential
energy* $U(\boldsymbol\xi)$ is the negative log posterior, and the ideal dynamics conserve their sum; the
small error from simulating the roll on a computer is what the final accept-reject step corrects. In one
line: this is what runs when you call Stan on a network meta-analysis, and everything below proves that
the roll-and-correct recipe targets the right distribution.

::: {#def-hmc}
## Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
To sample $\pi(\boldsymbol\xi \mid \mathbf y)$ on $\boldsymbol\xi \in \mathbb{R}^d$, augment the state
with an auxiliary momentum $\mathbf r \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and define the *Hamiltonian*
$$
H(\boldsymbol\xi, \mathbf r) = U(\boldsymbol\xi) + K(\mathbf r), \qquad
U(\boldsymbol\xi) = -\log \pi(\boldsymbol\xi \mid \mathbf y), \qquad
K(\mathbf r) = \tfrac12 \mathbf r^\top M^{-1}\mathbf r,
$$ {#eq-hamiltonian}
with a symmetric positive definite *mass matrix* $M$. The joint density $p(\boldsymbol\xi, \mathbf r)
\propto e^{-H(\boldsymbol\xi, \mathbf r)} = \pi(\boldsymbol\xi \mid \mathbf y)\,\mathcal{N}(\mathbf r;
\mathbf 0, M)$ has the target as its $\boldsymbol\xi$-marginal. One HMC transition from
$(\boldsymbol\xi, \mathbf r)$ is:

1. *Momentum refresh:* draw $\mathbf r \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf 0, M)$.
2. *Simulate dynamics:* approximate the Hamiltonian flow of
   $$
   \dot{\boldsymbol\xi} = \nabla_{\mathbf r} H = M^{-1}\mathbf r, \qquad
   \dot{\mathbf r} = -\nabla_{\boldsymbol\xi} H = \nabla_{\boldsymbol\xi} \log \pi(\boldsymbol\xi \mid \mathbf y),
   $$
   for $L$ steps of size $\epsilon$ using the *leapfrog* integrator
   $$
   \mathbf r^{+} = \mathbf r + \tfrac{\epsilon}{2}\nabla\log\pi(\boldsymbol\xi), \quad
   \boldsymbol\xi' = \boldsymbol\xi + \epsilon M^{-1}\mathbf r^{+}, \quad
   \mathbf r' = \mathbf r^{+} + \tfrac{\epsilon}{2}\nabla\log\pi(\boldsymbol\xi'),
   $$
   producing a proposal $(\boldsymbol\xi^{*}, \mathbf r^{*})$ (after negating the final momentum).
3. *Metropolis correction:* accept $(\boldsymbol\xi^{*}, \mathbf r^{*})$ with probability $\min\{1,
   \exp(H(\boldsymbol\xi, \mathbf r) - H(\boldsymbol\xi^{*}, \mathbf r^{*}))\}$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The correctness of HMC rests on three facts about the Hamiltonian flow and its leapfrog discretization,
which we prove, after which the Metropolis correction delivers the target by the detailed-balance
argument of @sec-mcmc.

::: {#lem-hamiltonian-conservation}
## The Hamiltonian flow conserves energy
Along any solution of Hamilton's equations $\dot{\boldsymbol\xi} = \nabla_{\mathbf r}H$, $\dot{\mathbf
r} = -\nabla_{\boldsymbol\xi}H$, the Hamiltonian $H$ is constant in time.
:::

::: {.proof}
By the chain rule and Hamilton's equations,
$$
\frac{dH}{dt} = \nabla_{\boldsymbol\xi}H \cdot \dot{\boldsymbol\xi} + \nabla_{\mathbf r}H \cdot \dot{\mathbf r}
= \nabla_{\boldsymbol\xi}H \cdot \nabla_{\mathbf r}H + \nabla_{\mathbf r}H \cdot (-\nabla_{\boldsymbol\xi}H) = 0. \qquad \square
$$
:::

::: {#lem-leapfrog-volume}
## The leapfrog map preserves volume and is reversible
The leapfrog map $(\boldsymbol\xi, \mathbf r) \mapsto (\boldsymbol\xi', \mathbf r')$ of @def-hmc has
Jacobian determinant equal to $1$, and is reversible: negating the momentum, applying the map, and
negating the momentum again recovers the inverse map.
:::

::: {.proof}
The map is the composition of three shears. The first, $(\boldsymbol\xi, \mathbf r) \mapsto
(\boldsymbol\xi, \mathbf r^{+})$ with $\mathbf r^{+} = \mathbf r + \frac{\epsilon}{2}\nabla\log\pi(
\boldsymbol\xi)$, leaves $\boldsymbol\xi$ fixed and updates $\mathbf r$ by a function of
$\boldsymbol\xi$ alone; its Jacobian in block form is $\left(\begin{smallmatrix} I & 0 \\ * & I
\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, lower triangular with unit diagonal, so its determinant is $1$. The second,
$(\boldsymbol\xi, \mathbf r^{+}) \mapsto (\boldsymbol\xi', \mathbf r^{+})$ with $\boldsymbol\xi' =
\boldsymbol\xi + \epsilon M^{-1}\mathbf r^{+}$, updates $\boldsymbol\xi$ by a function of $\mathbf r^{+}$
alone; its Jacobian is $\left(\begin{smallmatrix} I & * \\ 0 & I \end{smallmatrix}\right)$, again unit
determinant. The third is another momentum shear, determinant $1$. The determinant of the composition is
the product, $1 \cdot 1 \cdot 1 = 1$, so the leapfrog map preserves Lebesgue volume. Reversibility is
direct: each substep is inverted by running it with $\epsilon \mapsto -\epsilon$, and negating $\mathbf
r$ turns the forward half-steps into the corresponding backward half-steps, so the momentum-flip
conjugate of the leapfrog map is its own inverse. $\square$
:::

::: {#prp-hmc-invariance}
## HMC leaves the joint distribution invariant
The HMC transition of @def-hmc is reversible with respect to the joint density $p(\boldsymbol\xi,
\mathbf r) \propto e^{-H(\boldsymbol\xi, \mathbf r)}$, and therefore leaves the target posterior
$\pi(\boldsymbol\xi \mid \mathbf y)$ invariant as the $\boldsymbol\xi$-marginal.
:::

::: {.proof}
The momentum refresh draws $\mathbf r \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf 0, M)$, which is exactly the conditional
$p(\mathbf r \mid \boldsymbol\xi)$ under the joint $e^{-H}$, so it leaves the joint invariant. The
leapfrog proposal is a deterministic, volume-preserving (@lem-leapfrog-volume) involution after the
momentum flip. For such a proposal the two ingredients of the general acceptance ratio @eq-mh-acceptance
each simplify: the involution makes the forward map and its reverse identical after the momentum flip, so
the proposal is symmetric and the factor $q(y,x)/q(x,y)$ equals $1$; and volume preservation means the
change-of-variables Jacobian relating the forward and reverse densities is also $1$, so no Jacobian factor
survives. The acceptance ratio therefore collapses to the pure density ratio
$$
\frac{p(\boldsymbol\xi^{*}, \mathbf r^{*})}{p(\boldsymbol\xi, \mathbf r)} = \frac{e^{-H(\boldsymbol\xi^{*}, \mathbf r^{*})}}{e^{-H(\boldsymbol\xi, \mathbf r)}}
= \exp\!\bigl(H(\boldsymbol\xi, \mathbf r) - H(\boldsymbol\xi^{*}, \mathbf r^{*})\bigr),
$$
because the proposal Jacobian is $1$ and the involution makes the forward and reverse proposal densities
equal; this is the acceptance probability in step 3. By the detailed-balance computation of
@thm-mh-stationarity applied to the joint target $e^{-H}$, the accept-reject step is reversible with
respect to $e^{-H}$, so the joint distribution is invariant. (If the leapfrog flow were exact, energy
conservation @lem-hamiltonian-conservation would make $H(\boldsymbol\xi^{*}, \mathbf r^{*}) =
H(\boldsymbol\xi, \mathbf r)$ and every proposal would be accepted; finite $\epsilon$ introduces an
energy error that the Metropolis step corrects exactly.) Marginalizing the invariant joint over the
Gaussian momentum returns $\pi(\boldsymbol\xi \mid \mathbf y)$. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
HMC still requires the user to choose the trajectory length $L$ and step size $\epsilon$. The
*No-U-Turn Sampler* (NUTS) of @hoffman2014nuts eliminates the choice of $L$ by building the
leapfrog trajectory forward and backward in time, doubling its length until it begins to double back on
itself (formally, until the running trajectory would make a "U-turn," detected when the momentum becomes
anti-aligned with the position displacement), then selecting the next state from the trajectory by a
slice or multinomial rule that preserves detailed balance. The step size $\epsilon$ is tuned during a
warmup phase by dual averaging to hit a target acceptance rate near $0.8$, and the mass matrix $M$ is
adapted to the posterior covariance. NUTS is the default in Stan (@carpenter2017stan) and underlies the
multilevel models of Part V; the geometric foundations are surveyed by @betancourt2017 and
@neal2011hmc. A hierarchical-model caution connects back to this chapter, and it is the single most common practical
failure in Bayesian meta-analysis. In the centered parameterization $\theta_j \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu,
\tau^2)$, the joint posterior of $(\theta_j, \log\tau)$ has a *funnel* geometry: when $\tau$ is large the
study effects $\theta_j$ are free to spread out, but when $\tau$ is small they are squeezed into a narrow
neck around $\mu$. Picture a funnel or a trumpet bell, wide at the top and pinched at the bottom. A single
leapfrog step size cannot fit both regions at once; a step tuned for the wide mouth overshoots the narrow
neck, the simulated energy blows up, and the proposal is rejected as a *divergent transition*. The sampler
then silently fails to explore small $\tau$, biasing the posterior for $\tau$ upward and so overstating
heterogeneity.
The remedy is the *non-centered parameterization* $\theta_j = \mu + \tau\,\tilde\theta_j$ with
$\tilde\theta_j \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$, which factors the dependence out so that the geometry the sampler
actually traverses is a fixed unit Gaussian regardless of $\tau$; this is the standard fix and the reason
production NMA code is written in the non-centered form. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Marginal likelihood and Bayes factors {#sec-marginal-likelihood}

Model comparison uses the same marginal likelihood that normalizes the posterior, now read as a function
of the model.

::: {#def-marginal-likelihood}
## Marginal likelihood and Bayes factor
For a model $\mathcal{M}$ with parameter $\boldsymbol\xi$, prior $\pi(\boldsymbol\xi \mid \mathcal{M})$,
and likelihood $p(\mathbf y \mid \boldsymbol\xi, \mathcal{M})$, the *marginal likelihood* (or evidence)
is
$$
p(\mathbf y \mid \mathcal{M}) = \int p(\mathbf y \mid \boldsymbol\xi, \mathcal{M})\, \pi(\boldsymbol\xi \mid \mathcal{M})\, d\boldsymbol\xi.
$$
The *Bayes factor* comparing models $\mathcal{M}_1$ and $\mathcal{M}_0$ is the ratio of their marginal
likelihoods,
$$
\mathrm{BF}_{10} = \frac{p(\mathbf y \mid \mathcal{M}_1)}{p(\mathbf y \mid \mathcal{M}_0)}.
$$
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#prp-posterior-odds}
## Posterior odds equal the Bayes factor times prior odds
Given prior model probabilities $\pi(\mathcal{M}_0), \pi(\mathcal{M}_1) > 0$,
$$
\frac{P(\mathcal{M}_1 \mid \mathbf y)}{P(\mathcal{M}_0 \mid \mathbf y)}
= \mathrm{BF}_{10} \cdot \frac{\pi(\mathcal{M}_1)}{\pi(\mathcal{M}_0)}.
$$
:::

::: {.proof}
Treat the model index $\mathcal{M}$ as a discrete parameter and apply Bayes' theorem (@thm-bayes) at the
model level: $P(\mathcal{M}_k \mid \mathbf y) = p(\mathbf y \mid \mathcal{M}_k)\,\pi(\mathcal{M}_k)/
p(\mathbf y)$, where $p(\mathbf y) = \sum_k p(\mathbf y \mid \mathcal{M}_k)\pi(\mathcal{M}_k)$ is common
to both. Taking the ratio for $k = 1$ and $k = 0$ cancels $p(\mathbf y)$:
$$
\frac{P(\mathcal{M}_1 \mid \mathbf y)}{P(\mathcal{M}_0 \mid \mathbf y)}
= \frac{p(\mathbf y \mid \mathcal{M}_1)\,\pi(\mathcal{M}_1)}{p(\mathbf y \mid \mathcal{M}_0)\,\pi(\mathcal{M}_0)}
= \mathrm{BF}_{10}\cdot \frac{\pi(\mathcal{M}_1)}{\pi(\mathcal{M}_0)}. \qquad \square
$$
:::

::: {.remark}
The Bayes factor is the factor by which the data update the prior odds, and it is the principled
Bayesian model-comparison criterion. It is, however, sensitive to the prior on $\boldsymbol\xi$ within
each model, because $p(\mathbf y \mid \mathcal{M}) = \mathbb{E}_{\pi}[p(\mathbf y \mid \boldsymbol\xi)]$
averages the likelihood over the prior and so depends on prior mass placed in regions of low likelihood;
a diffuse prior can drive the marginal likelihood toward zero and favor the simpler model regardless of
the data, the phenomenon known as Lindley's paradox. The mechanism is spreading too thin: a prior
stretched over a very wide range places only a sliver of its mass near the parameter values the data
support, so the average of the likelihood over the prior, which is precisely what $p(\mathbf y \mid
\mathcal{M})$ computes, comes out small even when the best-fitting parameter value fits the data well. For this reason applied Bayesian model comparison
often prefers predictive criteria such as the widely applicable information criterion or
leave-one-out cross-validation, which are developed in the Bayesian-computation chapter of Part V. (
Corresponds to L.5 in the proof catalogue.) $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## A fully worked example {#sec-hb-worked}

We compute a three-study normal-normal meta-analysis entirely by hand: the shrinkage estimates, their
credible intervals, the empirical-Bayes heterogeneity, a direct conjugacy check, and one
Metropolis-Hastings acceptance probability.

::: {#exm-three-study-shrinkage}
## Partial pooling of three studies
Three trials report log-odds-ratio estimates
$$
y_1 = 0.0, \qquad y_2 = 0.6, \qquad y_3 = 1.2,
$$
each with the same known sampling variance $s_j^2 = 0.25$ (standard error $0.5$).

**Shrinkage with given hyperparameters.** Take the population mean $\mu = 0.6$ and between-study
variance $\tau^2 = 0.25$. The shrinkage factor of @eq-shrinkage is the same for all three studies,
$$
B_j = \frac{s_j^2}{s_j^2 + \tau^2} = \frac{0.25}{0.25 + 0.25} = \frac12,
$$
so $\hat\theta_j = \tfrac12\mu + \tfrac12 y_j$. The partial-pooling estimates are
$$
\hat\theta_1 = \tfrac12(0.6) + \tfrac12(0.0) = 0.30, \quad
\hat\theta_2 = \tfrac12(0.6) + \tfrac12(0.6) = 0.60, \quad
\hat\theta_3 = \tfrac12(0.6) + \tfrac12(1.2) = 0.90,
$$
each pulled halfway from its raw value toward the population mean $0.6$. The common posterior variance is
$V_j = (1 - B_j)s_j^2 = \tfrac12 \times 0.25 = 0.125$, with posterior standard deviation $\sqrt{0.125} =
0.35355$. The $95\%$ credible interval for $\theta_1$ is therefore
$$
0.30 \pm 1.96 \times 0.35355 = 0.30 \pm 0.6930 = (-0.393,\; 0.993).
$$

**Reading the result on the odds-ratio scale.** Translating back to the scale a clinician reads makes the
effect of shrinkage concrete. Trial 3's raw log odds ratio of $1.2$ (an odds ratio of $e^{1.2} = 3.32$)
shrinks to $0.90$ (an odds ratio of $e^{0.90} = 2.46$): partial pooling has walked the most eye-catching
trial back from roughly a tripling of the odds to about a $2.5$-fold effect, because that trial is one
imprecise result among three. For trial 1 the shrunken estimate $0.30$ corresponds to an odds ratio of
$e^{0.30} = 1.35$, and its credible interval $(-0.393,\; 0.993)$ becomes $(e^{-0.393},\; e^{0.993}) =
(0.67,\; 2.70)$ on the odds-ratio scale. That interval straddles $1$, so even after borrowing strength the
evidence for trial 1's population remains consistent with no effect: shrinkage has changed the point
estimate without manufacturing certainty.

**Direct conjugacy check.** Verify $\hat\theta_1$ from first principles by @thm-conjugate-normal. The
prior is $\theta_1 \sim \mathcal{N}(0.6, 0.25)$ and the likelihood is $y_1 = 0 \sim \mathcal{N}(\theta_1,
0.25)$. Posterior precision $= 1/0.25 + 1/0.25 = 4 + 4 = 8$, so $V_1 = 1/8 = 0.125$, matching above.
Posterior mean $= V_1(\mu/\tau^2 + y_1/s_1^2) = 0.125\,(0.6/0.25 + 0/0.25) = 0.125 \times 2.4 = 0.30$,
matching $\hat\theta_1$.

**Empirical Bayes by the DerSimonian-Laird estimator.** Now estimate $(\mu, \tau^2)$ from the data via
@eq-dersimonian-laird. The weights are $w_j = 1/s_j^2 = 4$, so $\sum_j w_j = 12$, the weighted mean is
$\bar y_w = (4 \cdot 0 + 4 \cdot 0.6 + 4 \cdot 1.2)/12 = 7.2/12 = 0.60$, and
$$
Q = \sum_j w_j (y_j - \bar y_w)^2 = 4\bigl[(0 - 0.6)^2 + 0 + (1.2 - 0.6)^2\bigr] = 4(0.36 + 0.36) = 2.88.
$$
With $J - 1 = 2$, $\sum_j w_j^2 = 3 \times 16 = 48$, and $\sum_j w_j^2/\sum_j w_j = 48/12 = 4$, the
denominator is $12 - 4 = 8$, so
$$
\hat\tau^2_{\mathrm{DL}} = \frac{2.88 - 2}{8} = \frac{0.88}{8} = 0.11.
$$
The estimated heterogeneity is smaller than the $\tau^2 = 0.25$ assumed above, so empirical Bayes shrinks
more aggressively: $\hat B_j = 0.25/(0.25 + 0.11) = 0.25/0.36 = 0.6944$, giving
$$
\hat\theta_1 = 0.6944(0.6) + 0.3056(0.0) = 0.4167, \quad
\hat\theta_2 = 0.60, \quad
\hat\theta_3 = 0.6944(0.6) + 0.3056(1.2) = 0.7833.
$$

**One Metropolis-Hastings step.** Suppose we sample the posterior $\theta_1 \mid y_1 \sim
\mathcal{N}(0.30, 0.125)$ of the first display by random-walk Metropolis with a symmetric Gaussian
proposal, so $q(x, y) = q(y, x)$ and the acceptance probability @eq-mh-acceptance reduces to $\min\{1,
\pi(y)/\pi(x)\}$. From the current state $\theta = 0.30$ (the posterior mode) propose $\theta' = 0.70$.
Then
$$
\frac{\pi(\theta')}{\pi(\theta)} = \exp\!\left(-\frac{(0.70 - 0.30)^2 - (0.30 - 0.30)^2}{2 \times 0.125}\right)
= \exp\!\left(-\frac{0.16}{0.25}\right) = e^{-0.64} = 0.5273,
$$
so the move is accepted with probability $0.5273$. A draw below this threshold accepts $\theta' = 0.70$;
otherwise the chain stays at $0.30$. Iterating such steps produces a sample from $\mathcal{N}(0.30,
0.125)$ by @thm-mh-stationarity. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#exm-beta-binomial-shrinkage}
## Beta-binomial shrinkage
A binary endpoint yields $y = 8$ successes in $n = 10$ patients, with a weakly informative prior $p \sim
\mathrm{Beta}(2, 2)$ (prior mean $0.5$, two pseudo-successes and two pseudo-failures). By
@thm-conjugate-beta-binomial the posterior is $\mathrm{Beta}(2 + 8, 2 + 2) = \mathrm{Beta}(10, 4)$, with
posterior mean
$$
\frac{10}{14} = 0.7143 = \frac{4}{14}\cdot \frac{2}{4} + \frac{10}{14}\cdot \frac{8}{10},
$$
a convex combination shrinking the maximum likelihood estimate $0.80$ toward the prior mean $0.50$, with
weight $10/14$ on the data. The posterior standard deviation is $\sqrt{10 \cdot 4/(14^2 \cdot 15)} =
\sqrt{40/2940} = 0.1167$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## The bridge to Bayesian network meta-analysis {#sec-hb-bridge}

The random-effects meta-analysis model @eq-normal-normal-model is the one-comparison special case of the
hierarchical models that drive the rest of this book. In a network of trials comparing several
treatments, each study $j$ contributes one or more relative-effect estimates, and the study-specific
true contrasts $\delta_{j,1k}$ (treatment $k$ versus the reference) are modeled as exchangeable draws
from a common distribution,
$$
\delta_{j,1k} \mid d_{1k}, \tau^2 \sim \mathcal{N}(d_{1k}, \tau^2),
$$
where $d_{1k}$ is the population (pooled) relative effect to be estimated and $\tau^2$ is the
between-study heterogeneity (@dias2018nma). This is precisely @def-hierarchical-model with the study
contrasts as unit parameters; the pooled effects $d_{1k}$ play the role of $\mu$, and the consistency
equations of the network tie the contrasts together algebraically. Because the link is typically the
logit and the likelihood binomial, the posterior is non-conjugate, and estimation proceeds by the
Hamiltonian Monte Carlo of @sec-hmc, as implemented in the Bayesian NMA software of Part III and the
multilevel network meta-regression of Part V. The shrinkage, REML, empirical-Bayes, and MCMC machinery
built here is the computational substrate of every Bayesian estimate reported in those chapters; the
non-collapsibility of the logit link (@def-non-collapsibility) is the reason the population and
study-level effects must be handled with the care this chapter develops.

## Notes and references {#sec-hb-notes}

The hierarchical and Bayesian material of this chapter is standard, and our presentation aligns with the
companion proof catalogue, where it is items L.1 through L.5: Bayes' theorem (L.1, @thm-bayes),
conjugate families (L.2, @thm-conjugate-normal, @thm-conjugate-beta-binomial,
@prp-conjugate-gamma-poisson), the Hamiltonian Monte Carlo invariance and the Metropolis-Hastings
detailed-balance argument (L.3, @thm-mh-stationarity, @prp-hmc-invariance, @def-hmc), the posterior
predictive distribution (L.4, @def-posterior-predictive), and the marginal likelihood and Bayes factors
(L.5, @def-marginal-likelihood, @prp-posterior-odds). The catalogue's one-line sketches have been
expanded into full proofs; in particular the Metropolis-Hastings stationarity is proved here from the
general detailed-balance lemma (@lem-detailed-balance-stationary) on a general state space, and the HMC
volume-preservation and energy-conservation facts (@lem-leapfrog-volume, @lem-hamiltonian-conservation)
are given complete proofs rather than cited. We additionally own the random-effects and REML content of
the chapter assignment: exchangeability and de Finetti (@def-exchangeability, @thm-de-finetti), the
hierarchical model and the random-versus-fixed distinction (@def-hierarchical-model,
@def-random-effects), the shrinkage estimator (@thm-shrinkage-posterior-mean), the James-Stein
phenomenon (@lem-stein, @thm-james-stein), and restricted maximum likelihood (@def-reml,
@thm-reml-invariance, @thm-reml-one-sample), together with the method-of-moments derivation of the
DerSimonian-Laird heterogeneity estimator (@prp-dl-moment).

The random-effects meta-analysis model and its Bayesian estimation follow @dias2018nma, which is the
primary source for the bridge in @sec-hb-bridge and for the practice of fitting these models by Markov
chain Monte Carlo. The method-of-moments heterogeneity estimator @eq-dersimonian-laird is from
@dersimonian1986, and we give its method-of-moments derivation in full (@prp-dl-moment) rather than
merely displaying the formula. The Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and No-U-Turn material, including the dual-averaging step
adaptation and the centered-versus-non-centered parameterization, follows @carpenter2017stan. The
linear-algebra prerequisites are the four fundamental subspaces and rank-nullity (@thm-four-subspaces,
@thm-rank-nullity), orthogonal projection and Gram-Schmidt (@def-projection-matrix, @thm-gram-schmidt),
and positive definiteness and quadratic forms (@thm-pd-characterization, @def-quadratic-form), all from
@strang2016; the multivariate normal facts (@thm-mvn-linear, @thm-mvn-conditional, @prp-mvn-density,
@def-conditional-independence) are from Chapter 4, and the variance-component and generalized
least squares background from @bingham2010regression. The primary sources are @definetti1937 and
@hewitt1955 for @thm-de-finetti; @stein1956, @james1961, and @efron1975 for @thm-james-stein;
@patterson1971 and @harville1977 for REML; @metropolis1953, @hastings1970, and @tierney1994 for
@sec-mcmc; and @hoffman2014nuts, @neal2011hmc, and @betancourt2017 for @sec-hmc.

No result in this chapter carries a machine-checked tag. The companion Coq development formalizes the
identification and algebraic content of the indirect-comparison methods, not Bayesian inference: there
is no Coq counterpart to the posterior, the conjugate updates, or the samplers, a scope decision
recorded in the companion manuscript. The cleanest candidates for future formalization are the purely
algebraic results here, namely the detailed-balance lemma (@lem-detailed-balance-stationary), the
shrinkage identity (@thm-shrinkage-posterior-mean), and the leapfrog volume-preservation
(@lem-leapfrog-volume).

## Exercises {#sec-hb-exercises}

A starred exercise ($\star$) has a full worked solution in Appendix F. The first two exercises are
plain-language warm-ups; the rest build up to the computations and proofs.

::: {#exr-interpret-shrinkage}
## Warm-up: reading shrinkage in words (interpretation)
No calculation is required. (a) Two trials estimate the same treatment contrast; trial A has a small
standard error and trial B a large one. In a random-effects meta-analysis, which of the two raw estimates
is pulled harder toward the pooled mean, and why? (b) Explain in one sentence each what it means for the
between-study variance to be $\tau^2 = 0$ and for $\tau^2$ to be very large, in terms of how much the
trials borrow strength. (c) A colleague reports a shrinkage factor $B_j = 0.8$ for a study and says
"good, that means we trust the study a lot." Correct the misunderstanding: what does $B_j = 0.8$ actually
say about that study, and which direction does it pull the estimate?
:::

::: {#exr-or-interpretation}
## Warm-up: from log odds ratios to a clinical statement (interpretation)
A Bayesian meta-analysis reports, for a treatment contrast on the log-odds-ratio scale, a posterior mean
of $0.55$ with a $95\%$ credible interval $(0.10,\; 1.00)$. (a) Convert the point estimate and both
interval endpoints to the odds-ratio scale. (b) State in one plain sentence what the credible interval
says, and contrast that with the (incorrect) confidence-interval interpretation a reader might reach for.
(c) Does the interval provide evidence of a treatment effect on the odds scale? Answer by reference to the
value $\mathrm{OR} = 1$.
:::

::: {#exr-shrinkage-unequal}
## Shrinkage with unequal variances
Two studies report $y_1 = 1.0$ with $s_1^2 = 0.04$ and $y_2 = 0.0$ with $s_2^2 = 0.36$, and the
hyperparameters are $\mu = 0.4$, $\tau^2 = 0.16$. (a) Compute the shrinkage factors $B_1, B_2$, the
partial-pooling estimates $\hat\theta_1, \hat\theta_2$, and the posterior variances $V_1, V_2$ from
@eq-shrinkage. (b) Explain, by comparing $B_1$ and $B_2$, why the less precise study is shrunk more.
(c) Give the $95\%$ credible interval for each $\theta_j$.
:::

::: {#exr-conjugate-n-sample}
## The $n$-sample normal update and complete pooling
For $y_1, \dots, y_n \mid \theta \sim \mathcal{N}(\theta, \sigma^2)$ iid with prior $\theta \sim
\mathcal{N}(\mu_0, \tau_0^2)$, prove from @thm-conjugate-normal that the posterior precision is
$\tau_0^{-2} + n\sigma^{-2}$ and the posterior mean is the precision-weighted average of $\mu_0$ and
$\bar y$. Deduce that as $n \to \infty$ the posterior concentrates at $\bar y$ regardless of the prior,
and interpret this as the data overwhelming the prior.
:::

::: {#exr-gamma-poisson-mean}
## Gamma-Poisson posterior mean as shrinkage
Using @prp-conjugate-gamma-poisson, show that the posterior mean of $\lambda$ given $y_1, \dots, y_n$ is
$$
\mathbb{E}[\lambda \mid \mathbf y] = \frac{a + \sum_i y_i}{b + n} = \frac{b}{b + n}\cdot \frac{a}{b} + \frac{n}{b + n}\cdot \bar y,
$$
a convex combination of the prior mean $a/b$ and the sample mean $\bar y$. Identify the data weight and
its limit as $n \to \infty$.
:::

::: {#exr-mh-detailed-balance-discrete}
## Detailed balance on a finite chain
Let $\mathcal{X} = \{1, 2, 3\}$ and let $\pi = (0.2, 0.3, 0.5)$ be a target. Take the symmetric proposal
that picks one of the other two states with probability $1/2$ each, and apply Metropolis-Hastings.
(a) Write down the full $3 \times 3$ transition matrix $P$ with entries $P_{xy} = q_{xy}\alpha(x, y)$ off
the diagonal and the rejection mass on the diagonal. (b) Verify directly that $\pi_x P_{xy} = \pi_y
P_{yx}$ for all $x \ne y$. (c) Confirm $\pi P = \pi$, illustrating @lem-detailed-balance-stationary.
:::

::: {#exr-hpd-vs-equal-tailed}
## Equal-tailed and HPD intervals
For a posterior $\theta \mid \mathbf y \sim \mathcal{N}(m, v)$, show that the $95\%$ equal-tailed and
$95\%$ HPD intervals coincide and both equal $m \pm 1.96\sqrt{v}$, and explain using @prp-hpd-shortest
why the coincidence is special to symmetric unimodal posteriors. Then for a $\mathrm{Gamma}(2, 1)$
posterior, argue qualitatively that the HPD interval is shifted toward smaller values relative to the
equal-tailed interval.
:::

::: {#exr-leapfrog-jacobian}
## Leapfrog volume preservation in one dimension
For $d = 1$ and $M = 1$, write the leapfrog map $(\xi, r) \mapsto (\xi', r')$ of @def-hmc explicitly as
a function of $(\xi, r)$ for a smooth log target $\log\pi(\xi)$, compute the $2 \times 2$ Jacobian
matrix, and verify its determinant equals $1$, confirming @lem-leapfrog-volume in this case.
:::

::: {#exr-empirical-bayes-recompute}
## Recomputing the worked example
Redo @exm-three-study-shrinkage with $y = (0.2, 0.5, 1.1)$ and common $s_j^2 = 0.20$. (a) Using $\mu =
0.6$, $\tau^2 = 0.20$, compute the shrinkage factor, the three partial-pooling estimates, and the
posterior standard deviation. (b) Compute the DerSimonian-Laird estimate $\hat\tau^2_{\mathrm{DL}}$ from
@eq-dersimonian-laird and the corresponding empirical-Bayes estimates. (c) Carry out one
Metropolis-Hastings acceptance-probability calculation for the posterior of $\theta_3$ with a proposed
move of your choice.
:::

::: {#exr-james-stein-sure}
## James-Stein dominance via the unbiased risk estimate ($\star$)
Let $\mathbf Y \sim \mathcal{N}_J(\boldsymbol\theta, \sigma^2 I_J)$ with $J \ge 3$ and $\sigma^2$ known.
(a) Prove Stein's unbiased risk estimate: for $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta} = \mathbf Y + \mathbf g(\mathbf
Y)$ with $\mathbf g$ weakly differentiable and suitably integrable, $\mathbb{E}\|\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}
- \boldsymbol\theta\|^2 = \mathbb{E}[J\sigma^2 + 2\sigma^2\nabla\cdot\mathbf g(\mathbf Y) + \|\mathbf
g(\mathbf Y)\|^2]$, using @lem-stein coordinatewise. (b) Apply it to the James-Stein choice $\mathbf
g(\mathbf y) = -(J - 2)\sigma^2\mathbf y/\|\mathbf y\|^2$ to recover the risk identity of
@thm-james-stein, and identify the positive-part estimator $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}^{\mathrm{JS+}} =
(1 - (J-2)\sigma^2/\|\mathbf Y\|^2)_{+}\mathbf Y$ as a further improvement. (c) Explain in one paragraph
how this justifies the partial pooling of meta-analysis without invoking a subjective prior. *(Solution
in Appendix F.)*
:::

::: {#exr-reml-one-way}
## REML for the balanced one-way model ($\star$)
Consider the balanced one-way random-effects model $y_{ij} = \mu + \theta_i + \varepsilon_{ij}$, $i = 1,
\dots, I$, $j = 1, \dots, n$, with $\theta_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \tau^2)$ and $\varepsilon_{ij} \sim
\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$, all independent. (a) Using a maximal set of error contrasts orthogonal to
$\mathbf 1_{In}$, or otherwise, derive the REML estimators of $(\sigma^2, \tau^2)$ in terms of the
within-group and between-group mean squares $\mathrm{MS}_{\mathrm{W}}$ and $\mathrm{MS}_{\mathrm{B}}$.
(b) Show that the REML between-groups computation uses the denominator $I - 1$ (correcting for the
estimated grand mean), whereas the corresponding maximum likelihood computation uses $I$, and confirm
that REML reproduces the analysis-of-variance estimators. (c) State the condition under which the REML
estimate of $\tau^2$ is truncated at zero, and relate it to @eq-dersimonian-laird. *(Solution in
Appendix F.)*
:::
